assessment: There is NOT enough data to build sourced 5/20/50/80/95 percentile levels for single-ride (or longest-ride) distance by sex, let alone by age. What exists: (1) platform MEANS per ride (Garmin 28.6 mi overall with near-flat age curve 27-30 mi; Strava ~12.8 mi/20.6 km; old UK Strava sex split 41 vs 34 km in 2016 and 32 vs 28 km in 2017, i.e. women's mean about 83-88% of men's); (2) one small 2026 US survey giving TYPICAL-ride p10/p50/p90 = 2/5/20 mi among all adult cyclists; (3) Strava only publishes relative growth in century riders, never the base share; (4) a 2001 enthusiast poll with one visible longest-ride bin (11% at 91-105 mi). Nothing published gives the distribution of a cyclist's LONGEST ride or the share who have ever ridden 100 km / 100 mi, by sex. Cycling Level has no distance standard, only time-for-distance tables. A distance rank could only be built as an explicitly modelled estimate (e.g. lognormal anchored to the Garmin mean for 'dedicated riders' or the Troy Press p50/p90 for 'all cyclists', with a female scale factor ~0.85 from Strava UK), and the choice of reference population dominates the answer: a 100-mile ride is far above p95 of typical rides for any population here, but the percentile of 'longest-ever ride' is unknown. Recommend either labelling it as a milestone tier system (e.g. 25 mi / 50 mi / metric century / century / 200 km) or flagging percentiles as modelled, low confidence.
